ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction 106(3):657-69.
ref.fetchedWhat: PubMed abstract and the full text (PMC author manuscript, incl. Tables 1-4), 2026-11-04

abstractQuotes: Life-time cumulative probability estimates of dependence remission were 83.7% for nicotine, 90.6% for alcohol, 97.2% for cannabis and 99.2% for cocaine.
Half of the cases of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted approximately 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after dependence onset, respectively.
survey: National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC), Wave 1, run by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA); face-to-face computer-assisted interviews by US Census Bureau interviewers using the AUDADIS-IV.
who: US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18+, living in households and group quarters (e.g. college quarters, group homes, boarding houses); continental US, Alaska, Hawaii and DC. Blacks, Hispanics and ages 18–24 oversampled, then weighted. Response rate 81%.

everDependent.quote: the subsample of respondents with lifetime history of dependence on nicotine (n=6,937), alcohol (n=4,781), cannabis (n=530) or cocaine (n=408).

dependenceDefinition: DSM-IV dependence: 3 or more of the 7 criteria within a 12-month period, at any time in life.

remission.definition: No longer having ANY of the dependence criteria, for good as of the interview. It is not the same as abstinence: someone who still drinks or smokes but has none of the 7 dependence signs counts as remitted.
remission.minimumDuration: None fixed. The person reports the age when the symptoms 'finally stopped' and 'never started happening again' up to the interview; time to remission = that age minus the age dependence began.
remission.quote: “about how old were you when you finally stopped having any of these experiences (dependence criteria) with (name of drug)? By finally stopped, I mean they never started happening again.”

estimateType.answer: Projected, not observed. The 83.7/90.6/97.2/99.2% are lifetime cumulative probabilities from survival analysis (actuarial life-table method). People not yet remitted at interview are counted up to their current age (censored), and the curve projects what share would remit over a whole life.
estimateType.quote: These projections were obtained by the standard actuarial method

byTimeSinceOnset.note: Cumulative probability of remission, % (same survival curves).
byTimeSinceOnset.quote: The cumulative probability of remission a decade after onset of dependence was 18.4% for nicotine, 37.4% for alcohol, 66.2% for cannabis, and 75.8% for cocaine.

medianYearsToRemission.note: Years from dependence onset (not from first use) until half had remitted; 'approximately' in the paper.

treatment: not in fetched text. The paper does not report treatment use or how many remitted without treatment; treatment is not among the predictors in Tables 3–4.

findingsForMen.text: Men remitted at a lower rate than women for all four substances (adjusted hazard ratios: nicotine 0.81, alcohol 0.80, cannabis 0.64, cocaine 0.65). Ages 18–29 were less likely than 45+ to remit from alcohol (0.78) but more likely from cannabis (2.40) and cocaine (4.61).
findingsForMen.quote: Males were less likely than females to remit from dependence on all the substances assessed

otherPredictors: Lower remission with a personality disorder (alcohol, cannabis) or dependence on another drug; past alcohol dependence lowered remission from nicotine and cannabis. Each extra year of education raised nicotine remission by 10%. Mood and anxiety disorders showed no link.
authorsCaveats: Self-report: social desirability can lead to over-report of remission; recall bias over long intervals.
People in institutions, or who died or had severe consequences, were not sampled, which can overestimate remission.
No data on the number or length of remission episodes; remission and relapse can alternate.
authorsCaveatQuote: these estimates should be interpreted with caution given the irregular course of addictions punctuated by remissions and relapses.
unclear: Table 4 headers show 'Nicotine remission (N=1300)' and 'Alcohol remission (N=2008)'; the text does not say what these N count (likely those who remitted).

nicotine.basedOn: A 2001–02 national US survey interviewed 43,093 adults; 6,937 had ever been dependent on nicotine. From the ages they said they got hooked and finally lost all symptoms, researchers projected 83.7% get there in a lifetime.
nicotine.caveat: A projection, not a headcount. 'Out' means no dependence symptoms, not always nicotine-free. Only 18.4% got there within 10 years; half took about 26.

alcohol.basedOn: A 2001–02 national US survey interviewed 43,093 adults; 4,781 had ever been dependent on alcohol. From the ages they said they got hooked and finally lost all symptoms, researchers projected 90.6% get there in a lifetime.
alcohol.caveat: A projection, not a headcount. 'Out' means no dependence symptoms; many still drink. Only 37.4% got there within 10 years; half took about 14.

cannabis.basedOn: A 2001–02 national US survey interviewed 43,093 adults; 530 had ever been dependent on cannabis. From the ages they said they got hooked and finally lost all symptoms, researchers projected 97.2% get there in a lifetime.
cannabis.caveat: A projection from a small group of 530. 'Out' means no dependence symptoms, not always quitting. Half took about 6 years.

cocaine.basedOn: A 2001–02 national US survey interviewed 43,093 adults; 408 had ever been dependent on cocaine. From the ages they said they got hooked and finally lost all symptoms, researchers projected 99.2% get there in a lifetime.
cocaine.caveat: Small group, and people in prison, hospital or who died were not surveyed, so the true share is likely lower. Half took about 5 years.

pageWording: The hero line 'of people who were ever hooked … get out' is fair if read as 'are projected to get free of dependence symptoms at some point'. Safer: 'are expected to get free of it at some point in life'.
